**Charles Eric Leiserson** (born 1953) is a [computer scientist](/wiki/Computer_scientist "Computer scientist") and [professor](/wiki/Professor "Professor") at [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT). He specializes in the theory of [parallel computing](/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing") and [distributed computing](/wiki/Distributed_computing "Distributed computing").

Leiserson received a [Bachelor of Science](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in computer science and mathematics from [Yale University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") in 1975 and a [PhD](/wiki/PhD "PhD") degree in computer science from [Carnegie Mellon University](/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") in 1981, where his advisors were [Jon Bentley](/wiki/Jon_Bentley_(computer_scientist) "Jon Bentley (computer scientist)") and [H. After playing for St. Paul in the 1997 season, Drew was selected in the first round of the [1998 MLB draft](/wiki/1998_Major_League_Baseball_draft "1998 Major League Baseball draft"), fifth overall, by the [St. Louis Cardinals](/wiki/St._Louis_Cardinals "St. Louis Cardinals"). In June he signed a $7 million contract,[[5]](#cite_note-rs1998-5) then hit .316 through 26 games with the [Triple-A](/wiki/Triple-A_(baseball) "Triple-A (baseball)") [Memphis Redbirds](/wiki/Memphis_Redbirds "Memphis Redbirds"). He was recalled by the Cardinals and made his debut on September 8, 1998—the game in which teammate [Mark McGwire](/wiki/Mark_McGwire "Mark McGwire") broke the [single-season home run record](/wiki/1998_Major_League_Baseball_home_run_record_chase "1998 Major League Baseball home run record chase") previously held by [Roger Maris](/wiki/Roger_Maris "Roger Maris"). Drew's first [at bat](/wiki/At_bat "At bat"), in the sixth inning, resulted in a [strikeout](/wiki/Strikeout "Strikeout"), and he finished the night 0-for-2. He ended up going 15-for-36 (.417) during 1998, with five home runs.

On August 9, on what would have been Drew's first game in Philadelphia, he sat out, citing a bruised right hand. In an attempt to confuse the Philadelphia fans, he did not wear his own jersey that night, which instead was worn by bullpen catcher, Jeff Murphy. The attempt failed, however, and he was booed and heckled throughout [batting practice](/wiki/Batting_practice "Batting practice"). **Kuwait**,[[a]](#cite_note-16) officially the **State of Kuwait**,[[b]](#cite_note-17) is a country in [West Asia](/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia"). With a coastline of approximately 500 km (311 mi), it is situated at the head of the [Persian Gulf](/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") in the northeastern edge of the [Arabian Peninsula](/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"), bordering [Iraq](/wiki/Iraq "Iraq") to [the north](/wiki/Iraq%E2%80%93Kuwait_border "Iraq–Kuwait border") and [Saudi Arabia](/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") to [the south](/wiki/Kuwait%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_border "Kuwait–Saudi Arabia border").[[16]](#cite_note-cia-18) Kuwait is geographically the closest Gulf country to [mainland Iran](/wiki/Iranian_plateau "Iranian plateau") (separated only by a small [Iraqi coastline](/wiki/Al-Faw_peninsula "Al-Faw peninsula")).[[17]](#cite_note-19) The country is a small [city-state](/wiki/City-state "City-state");[[18]](#cite_note-20) most of the population reside in the [urban agglomeration](/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") of [Kuwait City](/wiki/Kuwait_City "Kuwait City"), the capital and largest city.[[19]](#cite_note-21) As of 2024, Kuwait has a population of 4.82 million, of which 1.53 million are [Kuwaiti citizens](/wiki/Kuwaiti_nationality_law "Kuwaiti nationality law") while the remaining 3.29 million are [foreign nationals](/wiki/Expatriates_in_Kuwait "Expatriates in Kuwait") from over 100 countries.[[20]](#cite_note-:1-22) In 2024, Kuwait had the world's seventh [largest number of foreign nationals as a percentage of the population](/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_by_immigrant_and_emigrant_population "List of sovereign states by immigrant and emigrant population"), where its citizens make up fewer than 30% of the overall population.[[21]](#cite_note-23)

The territory of modern-day Kuwait has been occupied by humans since antiquity, particularly due to its strategic location near the mouth of the [Tigris and Euphrates rivers](/wiki/Tigris%E2%80%93Euphrates_river_system "Tigris–Euphrates river system"). Robert Burns Woodward :: Research and career :: Organic syntheses and Nobel Prize :: part 02 :: chunk_0005
In the early 1950s, Woodward, along with the British chemist [Geoffrey Wilkinson](/wiki/Geoffrey_Wilkinson "Geoffrey Wilkinson"), then at Harvard, postulated a novel structure for [ferrocene](/wiki/Ferrocene "Ferrocene"), a compound consisting of a combination of an organic molecule with iron.[[9]](#cite_note-9) This marked the beginning of the field of [transition metal](/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal") [organometallic chemistry](/wiki/Organometallic_chemistry "Organometallic chemistry") which grew into an industrially very significant field.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Wilkinson won the Nobel Prize for this work in 1973, along with [Ernst Otto Fischer](/wiki/Ernst_Otto_Fischer "Ernst Otto Fischer").[[11]](#cite_note-11) Some historians think that Woodward should have shared this prize along with Wilkinson. Remarkably, Woodward himself thought so, and voiced his thoughts in a letter sent to the Nobel Committee.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Woodward won the Nobel Prize in 1965 for his synthesis of complex organic molecules. He had been nominated a total of 111 times from 1946 to 1965.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In his Nobel lecture, he described the total synthesis of the antibiotic cephalosporin, and claimed that he had pushed the synthesis schedule so that it would be completed around the time of the Nobel ceremony.

*Crocus* display the general characteristics of family [Iridaceae](/wiki/Iridaceae "Iridaceae"), which include basal cauline (arising from the aerial stem) leaves that sheath the stem base, [hermaphrodite](/wiki/Hermaphrodite "Hermaphrodite") flowers that are relatively large and showy, the perianth petaloid with two whorls of three tepals each and septal nectaries. The flowers have three stamens and a gynoecium of three united carpels and an inferior ovary, three locules and axile placentation with fruit that is a loculicidal capsule.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al1998295–296-2)

*Crocus* is an [acaulescent](/wiki/Acaulescent "Acaulescent") (lacking a visible lower stem above ground) diminutive seasonal cormous (growing from [corms](/wiki/Corm "Corm")) [herbaceous perennial](/wiki/Perennial_plant "Perennial plant") [geophytic](/wiki/Geophytic "Geophytic") genus.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeerow201223-3) The corms are symmetrical and [globose](/wiki/Globose "Globose") or [oblate](/wiki/Glossary_of_botanical_terms#oblate "Glossary of botanical terms") (round in shape with flatted tops and bottoms), and are covered with tunic leaves that are fibrous, membranous or [coriaceous](/wiki/Coriaceous "Coriaceous") (leathery). The corms produce fibrous [roots](/wiki/Root "Root"), and contractile roots which adjust the corms depth in the soil, which may be pulled as deep as 20 centimetres (8 in) into the soil.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al1998-4)[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZhao_et_al2004-5) The roots appear randomly from the lower part of the corm, but in a few species, from a basal ridge.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al1998297-6)

YouTube, a video sharing platform, has faced various criticisms over the years, particularly regarding [content moderation](/wiki/Content_moderation "Content moderation"), offensive content, and monetization. YouTube has faced criticism over aspects of its operations,[[236]](#cite_note-YouTube_moderation_Alexander-237) its [recommendation algorithms](/wiki/Recommender_system "Recommender system") perpetuating [videos that promote conspiracy theories](#Promotion_of_conspiracy_theories_and_fringe_discourse) and falsehoods,[[237]](#cite_note-238) hosting videos ostensibly targeting children but containing [violent or sexually suggestive content involving popular characters](/wiki/Elsagate "Elsagate"),[[238]](#cite_note-239) videos of minors attracting [pedophilic](/wiki/Pedophilia "Pedophilia") activities in their comment sections,[[239]](#cite_note-240) and fluctuating policies on the types of content that is eligible to be monetized with advertising.[[236]](#cite_note-YouTube_moderation_Alexander-237)

YouTube has also been blocked by several countries. As of 2018, public access to YouTube was blocked by countries including [China](/wiki/China "China"), [North Korea](/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), [Iran](/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [Turkmenistan](/wiki/Turkmenistan "Turkmenistan"),[[240]](#cite_note-241) [Uzbekistan](/wiki/Uzbekistan "Uzbekistan"),[[241]](#cite_note-242)[[242]](#cite_note-243) [Tajikistan](/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan"), [Eritrea](/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea"), [Sudan](/wiki/Sudan "Sudan") and [South Sudan](/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan").

North African campaign :: part 04 :: chunk_0003
The **North African campaign** of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") took place in [North Africa](/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa") from 11 June 1940 to 13 May 1943, fought between the [Allies](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") and the [Axis powers](/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"). It included campaigns in the [Libyan](/wiki/Italian_Libya "Italian Libya") and [Egyptian](/wiki/History_of_Egypt_under_the_British "History of Egypt under the British") deserts ([Western Desert campaign](/wiki/Western_Desert_campaign "Western Desert campaign"), Desert War), in [Morocco](/wiki/French_protectorate_in_Morocco "French protectorate in Morocco") and [Algeria](/wiki/French_Algeria "French Algeria") ([Operation Torch](/wiki/Operation_Torch "Operation Torch")), and in [Tunisia](/wiki/French_protectorate_of_Tunisia "French protectorate of Tunisia") ([Tunisia campaign](/wiki/Tunisian_campaign "Tunisian campaign")). The Allied war effort was dominated by the [British Commonwealth](/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") and exiles from [German-occupied Europe](/wiki/German-occupied_Europe "German-occupied Europe"). The United States entered the war in December 1941 and began direct military assistance in North Africa on 11 May 1942.

His father was sales manager of a wholesale shoe company,[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeiner2009-4) whose family was [Irish](/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") and, in about 1850, following the [Great Irish Famine](/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland) "Great Famine (Ireland)"), had emigrated to the U.S., first to [Massachusetts](/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") and later to California.[[8]](#cite_note-bnotes-8)

McNamara graduated from [Piedmont High School](/wiki/Piedmont_High_School_(California) "Piedmont High School (California)") in [Piedmont, California](/wiki/Piedmont,_California "Piedmont, California") in 1933, where he was president of the Rigma Lions boys club[[9]](#cite_note-9) and earned the rank of [Eagle Scout](/wiki/Eagle_Scout_(Boy_Scouts_of_America) "Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)"). According to McNamara, scouting helped him set his values and was where he first developed an interest in [public service](/wiki/Public_service "Public service").[[8]](#cite_note-bnotes-8)

McNamara attended the [University of California, Berkeley](/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") and graduated in 1937 with a [B.A.](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in [economics](/wiki/Economics "Economics") with minors in [mathematics](/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") and [philosophy](/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy"). Embiid was born in [Yaoundé](/wiki/Yaound%C3%A9 "Yaoundé"), [Cameroon](/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon"), to military officer Thomas Embiid[[8]](#cite_note-JConn-9) and his wife, Christine.[[9]](#cite_note-10) He played [volleyball](/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball") and [soccer](/wiki/Soccer "Soccer")[[10]](#cite_note-urlJoel_Embiid_shows_off_sick_footwork,_ball_skills_(in_soccer)_|_RSN-11) in childhood and originally planned to play professional volleyball in Europe[[11]](#cite_note-MDecourcy-12) but started playing basketball at age 15, modeling his game after NBA [Hall of Fame](/wiki/Naismith_Memorial_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame") center [Hakeem Olajuwon](/wiki/Hakeem_Olajuwon "Hakeem Olajuwon").[[8]](#cite_note-JConn-9)[[11]](#cite_note-MDecourcy-12) Embiid was discovered at a basketball camp by [Luc Mbah a Moute](/wiki/Luc_Mbah_a_Moute "Luc Mbah a Moute"), a fellow native of Yaoundé and an NBA player.[[11]](#cite_note-MDecourcy-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13) With Mbah a Moute as his mentor, Embiid moved to the United States at age 16 to devote himself to becoming a professional basketball player.[[13]](#cite_note-DTelep-14)

Embiid enrolled at [Montverde Academy](/wiki/Montverde_Academy "Montverde Academy"), Mbah a Moute's alma mater, but transferred after his first year due to a lack of playing time.[[11]](#cite_note-MDecourcy-12)[[14]](#cite_note-ljenkins1-15) He then attended The Rock School, a Christian academy, in [Gainesville, Florida](/wiki/Gainesville,_Florida "Gainesville, Florida").[[14]](#cite_note-ljenkins1-15) As a senior, he led their team to a 33–4 record and state championship, averaging 13.0 points, 9.7 rebounds and 1.9 blocks per game.

Embiid was a [five-star recruit](/wiki/College_recruiting#Star_ratings "College recruiting") according to [Rivals.com](/wiki/Rivals.com "Rivals.com")[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17) and committed to [Kansas](/wiki/Kansas_Jayhawks_men%27s_basketball "Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball") in November 2012.[[13]](#cite_note-DTelep-14)

The [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League"), known until 1992 as the European Champion Clubs' Cup or colloquially as the European Cup, is an annual [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") cup competition organised by [UEFA](/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") since 1955. Originally a straight knockout competition open only to champion clubs, the tournament was expanded during the 1990s to incorporate a round-robin group phase and more teams. The expansion resulted in more games being played, increasing players' goalscoring chances; thus the rankings are weighted in favour of modern players: only six out of the 50 players on the list never competed in the reformed Champions League.

With 140 goals, [Cristiano Ronaldo](/wiki/Cristiano_Ronaldo "Cristiano Ronaldo") is currently the all-time top scorer in the Champions League, with [Lionel Messi](/wiki/Lionel_Messi "Lionel Messi") and [Robert Lewandowski](/wiki/Robert_Lewandowski "Robert Lewandowski") being the only other players to have reached triple figures. Ronaldo has also finished as the top scorer [for the most individual seasons](#By_player) in the competition's history, doing so seven times.

The title of highest goalscorer had previously been held by [Raúl](/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_(footballer) "Raúl (footballer)"), who scored his 50th goal in 2005 while at [Real Madrid](/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF") to overtake [Alfredo Di Stéfano](/wiki/Alfredo_Di_St%C3%A9fano "Alfredo Di Stéfano").[[1]](#cite_note-1) He held the record until November 2014,[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) when his eventual tally of 71 was first equalled and then surpassed by Messi.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) Ronaldo has remained the competition's outright top scorer since September 2015; after a back-and-forth exchange of the record between him and Messi, a h

Tammy Baldwin :: U.S. House of Representatives (1999–2013) :: Elections :: chunk_0003
In 1998, U.S. Congressman [Scott Klug](/wiki/Scott_Klug "Scott Klug") of the [2nd district](/wiki/Wisconsin%27s_2nd_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 2nd congressional district"), based in Madison, announced he would retire, prompting Baldwin to run for the seat. Baldwin's ads leaned into the fact that Wisconsin had never sent a woman to Congress, and many of her ads targeted younger voters.[[20]](#cite_note-20) She won the Democratic primary with a plurality of 37% of the vote.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In the general election, she defeated Republican nominee Josephine Musser, 53–47%.[[22]](#cite_note-22) Baldwin's campaign drew strong turnout in [Dane County](/wiki/Dane_County,_Wisconsin "Dane County, Wisconsin"), using a team of volunteers, many of whom were students. The turnout was said to have helped [Russ Feingold's](/wiki/Russ_Feingold "Russ Feingold") reelection campaign [that year](/wiki/1998_United_States_Senate_election_in_Wisconsin "1998 United States Senate election in Wisconsin"), and was acknowledged by Feingold as a factor.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Baldwin is the first woman elected to Congress from Wisconsin. She is also the [first openly gay](/wiki/List_of_the_first_LGBT_holders_of_political_offices_in_the_United_States "List of the first LGBT holders of political offices in the United States") non-incumbent elected to the House of Representatives, and the first open lesbian elected to Congress.[[2]](#cite_note-Cogan2-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gay12-3) She and Representative [Barney Frank](/wiki/Barney_Frank "Barney Frank") co-founded the [Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus](/wiki/Congressional_LGBTQ%2B_Equality_Caucus "Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus") in 2008.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

In 2000, Baldwin was reelected, defeating Republican nominee John Sharpless by 8,902 votes (51%–49%). She lost eight of the district's nine counties, but carried the largest, Dane County, with 55% of the vote.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

Orville in flight over [Huffman Prairie](/wiki/Huffman_Prairie "Huffman Prairie") in [Wright Flyer II](/wiki/Wright_Flyer_II "Wright Flyer II"). Flight 85, approximately 1,760 feet (536 m) in 40+1⁄5 seconds, November 16, 1904

In 1904 the Wrights built the [Wright Flyer II](/wiki/Wright_Flyer_II "Wright Flyer II"). They decided to avoid the expense of travel and bringing supplies to the Outer Banks and set up an airfield at [Huffman Prairie](/wiki/Huffman_Prairie "Huffman Prairie"), a cow pasture eight miles 8 miles (13 km) northeast of Dayton. The Wrights referred to the airfield as Simms Station in their flying school brochure. They received permission to use the field rent-free from owner and bank president Torrance Huffman.

They invited reporters to their first flight attempt of the year on May 23, on the condition that no photographs be taken. Engine troubles and slack winds prevented any flying, and they could manage only a very short hop a few days later with fewer reporters present. Library of Congress historian Fred Howard noted some speculation that the brothers had intentionally failed to fly in order to cause reporters to lose interest in their experiments. Whether that is true is not known, but after their poor showing local newspapers virtually ignored them for the next year and a half.[[99]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoward1988154–155-102)

The Wrights were glad to be free from the distraction of reporters. The absence of newsmen also reduced the chance of competitors learning their methods. After the Kitty Hawk powered flights, the Wrights made a decision to begin withdrawing from the bicycle business so they could concentrate on creating and marketing a practical airplane.[[100]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouch2003273–274-103) This was financially risky, since they were neither wealthy nor government-funded (unlike other experimenters such as [Ader](/wiki/Cl%C3%A9ment_Ader "Clément Ader"), [Maxim](/wiki/Hiram_Stevens_Maxim "Hiram Stevens Maxim"
